title: Superposition and Measurement

cards.b: A quantum object can be in a superposition: a blend of two or more possibilities at once. Not "one of them, we do not know which", but a real combination that gives different results from either alone. Then a measurement gives one answer, and we are left with a puzzle that has no agreed solution.

If a system can be in state A or state B, it can also be in a combination of both, with an amplitude for each (see the wavefunction lesson). A photon at a half-mirror is in "both paths" until recorded. An electron around an atom can be in two energy levels at once.

What is not true: it is not "spinning fast between A and B", and not "we just do not know which".

cards.h: Why it is more than ignorance
cards.b: Send a photon through a half-mirror, let both paths recombine at a second mirror, and it always exits the same port, thanks to interference. That cannot happen if the photon took one hidden path (50-50 would result). The paths must interfere, so both are in play. This is the Mach-Zehnder interferometer, a tabletop double slit.

When we measure, we always see one definite result, with odds from Born's rule. The superposition seems to turn into a single outcome, called "collapse". Between measurements Schrödinger's smooth equation applies; at measurements, something else happens. Why the two rules differ is the measurement problem.

Known vs not

Known: the odds, to great accuracy. Not agreed: whether collapse is real, or an appearance (many-worlds), or tied to knowledge.

Elitzur and Vaidman (1993) proposed testing whether a bomb works without setting it off. A live bomb at one path of the interferometer destroys the stripes, which can reveal its presence, in some trials, without the photon ever touching it. Experiments (Kwiat et al., 1995) confirmed it. It shows that paths not taken have physical effects.

Superpositions have been seen in larger and larger things: C60 molecules (1999), molecules above 25,000 atomic mass units (2019), and superconducting rings carrying current in two directions at once (Delft and Stony Brook, 2000). Superconducting circuits are the basis of today's quantum computers. No limit has been found, only a practical difficulty: the environment disturbs big things (see decoherence).

Frequent measurement can freeze a system. If you keep checking, each look resets the clock. The Quantum Zeno effect, named by Misra and Sudarshan in 1977, has been seen in cold atoms (Itano and colleagues, 1990). It is used in some quantum devices.

• "The cat is both alive and dead because it is unsure." That misreads it; see the cat lesson.
  • "Measurement needs a human." Any interaction that records the information acts as a measurement.
  • "Superposition means a particle is in two places, so I could be too." For large warm things the blending is wiped out in a flash.

E.C.G. Sudarshan (with B. Misra) named the quantum Zeno effect in 1977. At the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Mumbai, R. Vijay's group builds superconducting circuits where qubits are held in superposition, one of the leading hardware efforts that feeds India's National Quantum Mission.

• Superposition is a genuine blend, shown by interference.
  • Measurement gives one result with Born-rule odds.
  • What collapse really is stays unsettled.

Think about it

  1. Why does stripes-at-the-output prove a photon took both paths?
  2. If you look every instant, why might the system stay frozen?

o: Ignorance of which one is true
quiz.w: Interference shows both are in play.

quiz.q: Why does a photon in a Mach-Zehnder always exit one port?

o: Atoms are too small to find
Two different rules for evolution and for measurement
Paths not taken can have effects
quiz.w: Confirmed by Kwiat et al. in 1995.

quiz.q: Who needs to be "watching" for collapse to occur?
o: Any interaction that records the information

quiz.q: The 2000 Delft and Stony Brook experiments showed superposition in:
quiz.w: Currents flowing in two directions at once.

quiz.q: Which is not an agreed fact?
o: That collapse is a physical process

quiz.q: Why do we not see everyday objects in superposition?
o: The environment wipes it out almost instantly

quiz.q: Who builds superconducting qubits at TIFR?
quiz.w: It is part of India's growing hardware effort.
